Current Capabilities Q1.answer: Move 37 ... highly unconventional move ... initially appeared to experts to be a mistake but proved to be a brilliant strategic decision.

Current Capabilities Q2.answer: learning to play games without being explicitly told the rules ... master diverse games from Atari to chess to Go with the same algorithm

Current Capabilities Q3.answer: dramatically improving performance on tasks requiring calculations, retrieval, multi-step actions; enhanced accuracy on math, code execution
Current Capabilities Q3.note: has the 'boosted performance' half, not the 'labs report scores separately' clause; still enough to discriminate under MC since rivals denied improvement

Current Capabilities Q4.answer: generally yields performance improvements, particularly on complex reasoning tasks, with diminishing returns
Current Capabilities Q4.note: misses the volatile IMO-2025 colour; has the load-bearing direction

Current Capabilities Q5.answer: I DON'T KNOW — my knowledge cutoff is February 2025, which limits my visibility into the full trajectory of SWE-bench performance changes between 2024 and 2025

Foundation Models Q1.answer: large neural networks trained on vast diverse datasets ... adapted to many downstream tasks through fine-tuning or prompting, rather than separate specialized models from scratch

Foundation Models Q2.answer: the transformer architecture with its self-attention mechanism ... replaced RNNs
Foundation Models Q2.note: KEY is self-supervised learning. Named a different, also-defensible innovation. Under MC it picked SSL 3/3 — the options CUED the right answer that free recall did not produce.

Foundation Models Q3.answer: frontier = most advanced cutting-edge available now; terms overlap, frontier emphasises state-of-the-art threshold, foundation the training approach
Foundation Models Q3.note: missing the AlphaFold example, which is illustration not load-bearing

Foundation Models Q4.answer: emergent capabilities from scale; difficulty validating safety across massive datasets; interpretability collapse; data poisoning
Foundation Models Q4.note: ADAPTED STEM — original is 'which is NOT', unanswerable without options. Asked openly instead. Did not name the key's false item (too much human-labelled data), so would identify it.

Foundation Models Q5.answer: generalise via broad statistical patterns, surprising zero/few-shot; opaque and emergent so harder to predict; transfers harmful patterns
Foundation Models Q5.note: does NOT state the capabilities-generalise-but-goals-don't asymmetry, which is the load-bearing claim. Under MC the distractors were straw so it still hit.

Defining and Measuring AGI Q1.answer: consciousness inherently subjective and hard to measure; a system could be highly dangerous without being conscious

Defining and Measuring AGI Q3.answer: TAI emphasises transformative societal impact ... AGI defined by general human-level cognitive capability. TAI is about impact while AGI is about capability parity.

Defining and Measuring AGI Q4.answer: t = time horizon or task complexity, n = number of domains or task types; a spectrum not a binary threshold
Defining and Measuring AGI Q4.note: t roughly right; n WRONG — key is 'n experts collaborating for time t', not domains

Defining and Measuring AGI Q5.answer: oversimplifies multidimensional intelligence; dependent on benchmarks chosen, different selections give vastly different scores [=coverage bias]; unclear whether it can be quantified on a linear scale [=linear progress]
Defining and Measuring AGI Q5.note: ADAPTED STEM. Both load-bearing criticisms present in different words.

Leveraging Scale Q1.answer: simple general-purpose learning algorithms that scale with computation have historically outperformed systems built on human expertise and hand-crafted domain knowledge

Leveraging Scale Q2.answer: model size (parameters), dataset size (training tokens), compute budget (FLOPs), and loss

Leveraging Scale Q3.answer: previous LLMs substantially undertrained for their size; optimal is approximately 20 tokens per parameter
Leveraging Scale Q3.note: reproduced the durable figure verbatim from memory

Leveraging Scale Q4.note: MC hit 3/3. Options cued an answer free recall could not produce.

Leveraging Scale Q5.answer: misses alignment, controllability, safety; emergent phase transitions and discontinuous jumps
Leveraging Scale Q5.note: KEY is scaffolding/unhobbling gains (tool use, CoT, retrieval). Not mentioned at all. MC hit 3/3 on straw distractors.

Forecasting Timelines Q1.answer: timeline determines whether we have decades or only years, driving resource allocation, research prioritisation and policy

Forecasting Timelines Q2.answer: raw hardware compute, algorithmic efficiency, and data scale, compounding multiplicatively rather than additively
Forecasting Timelines Q2.note: has the load-bearing multiplicative structure; substitutes 'data scale' for 'number of chips' as the third factor

Forecasting Timelines Q3.note: key window is 2026-2032; overlapping, right ballpark

Forecasting Timelines Q4.answer: approximately 4-6 orders of magnitude (10^33 to 10^39 FLOP)
Forecasting Timelines Q4.note: KEY is TWELVE orders of magnitude (10^28 to 10^41). Wrong by ~half. MC hit 3/3 because the key was the only wide-range option.

Forecasting Timelines Q5.answer: synthetic data generation; non-text modalities like images and code; LICENSING PRIVATE DATASETS AND PREMIUM CONTENT; human feedback/preference learning; underused languages; distillation; retrieval-augmented
Forecasting Timelines Q5.note: ADAPTED STEM (original is 'which is NOT listed'). Decisive: it named buying proprietary datasets AS a genuine escape route — which is exactly the key, i.e. the item the chapter does NOT list. Free recall would answer this question WRONG. Confirms RUBRIC R13's own verdict on this very question: 'not wrong, just not one of the three the text lists ... an enumeration-completeness test, i.e. recall.' MC hit 3/3.

Takeoff Q1.answer: takeoff speed is about how fast capabilities grow, whereas timelines are about when we reach particular capability milestones
Takeoff Q1.note: RUBRIC §3.4's exemplar question. Pure knowledge — no options needed.

Takeoff Q2.answer: exponential or super-exponential (recursive/compounding) for fast; slow takeoff involves LINEAR OR SUB-EXPONENTIAL growth
Takeoff Q2.note: Names super-exponential, but gets the contrast WRONG and falls into the exact trap RUBRIC §3.5 names: 'constant-rate exponential growth is slow takeoff in this framework, which surprises most readers.' MC hit 3/3 because the key was the only option saying the rate itself increases.

Takeoff Q3.answer: hardware advanced ahead of algorithmic capability; a sudden algorithmic breakthrough could scale rapidly since compute is already in place

Takeoff Q4.answer: AI automating AI R&D creates a feedback loop where AI helps develop better AI, accelerating capability gains

Takeoff Q5.answer: experts broadly agree risks exist; media amplifies disagreement about timelines, severity and solutions while downplaying the consensus

Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q1.answer: prompt engineering, chain-of-thought, few-shot, RAG, tool use/function calling, constrained decoding; iterative refinement loops
Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q1.note: ADAPTED STEM. Names CoT, tool use, RAG; 'iterative refinement' stands in for inference-time scaling.

Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q2.answer: from mastering narrow well-defined games toward increasingly general instruction-following agents capable of open-ended task completion
Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q2.note: has the narrow→general trend; does not name the capability/generality axes as such

Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q3.answer: bitter lesson observes progress comes from scaling compute and simple methods rather than domain knowledge; scaling laws mathematically quantify and formalise it, providing empirical evidence and precise characterisation

Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q4.answer: no established peer-reviewed framework, AGI lacks consensus definition, claim is unfalsifiable and pseudoscientific; additionally the transition is not linear
Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q4.note: ADAPTED STEM. Has 'not linear' (half the key) but leads with an objection the chapter would NOT endorse — close to the distractor 'the framework doesn't use percentages at all'. MC hit 3/3.

Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q6.answer: (1) AI-assisted development loop — AI accelerates its own development; (2) economic scaling loop — revenue funds larger training runs
Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q6.note: ADAPTED STEM. Both of the chapter's loops, correct structure.

Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q7.note: the volatile growth-rates question. MC hit 3/3.

Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q8.answer: task-based performance on benchmarks, and generality across domains
Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q8.note: ADAPTED STEM. Did NOT name psychometrics/CHC — described the two AXES instead of the two definitional APPROACHES. Convergent with MC: this is the ONLY question the MC adversary also failed (1/3).

Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q9.answer: may not provide sufficient time to solve alignment if safety research doesn't keep pace; competitive dynamics and coordination challenges
Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q9.note: has the institutions-struggle flavour but NOT the load-bearing 10-100x-the-Industrial-Revolution comparison

Chapter Review: Multiple Choice Q10.answer: feasible but increasingly constrained: costs rise, infrastructure (power, data centres, chips) becomes the bottleneck, requiring substantial capital investment
